title: Joining the union in 1933 and the 22nd Street boundary
summary: He joined after the Walkathons; black musicians could not work north of 22nd Street, and business agent Jaborotsky threatened club owners.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: But when did you first join the union? You had talked earlier about playing the Walkathons and the hustling gigs.
Yeah, right, right. Well, let's see, I think I first started joining the union when I -- in -- when I come to Chicago, here, in 193- -- yeah, about '33.
When you were through with the Walkathons.
Yeah, right, after I come back to Chicago, then I joined the union. Before, I didn't belong when we were hustling and things like that. Wasn't no cause, you know.
Well, did the union hassle you back in those days?

No, no, they didn't hassle. But if you wanted to work on the South Side, you would have had to be in the union. And when I say work on the South Side, they had boundaries at that time. This is before the merger or before anybody thought about the merger. They had boundaries. You couldn't work past -- black musicians couldn't work past 22nd
Yet some did, like Lee Collins, worked at the Victory Club.
This is not -- the point I'm talking about --
Right, right, and the '30s, the early part of the '30s. But, see, I'm talking about the average -- I mean, any kind of a choice club, those were strip joints.

Kelly's Stables had them for years. They had Johnny Dodds and Baby Dodds, and those people over there. But, I mean, they were just a few jobs, I mean, nothing like -- I'm talking about the hotels and no radio stations or nothing like that. And no regular bigtime jobs. Kelly's Stables considered a cabaret, a midnight, and that type of a thing, they let them do that.

But they had this boundary line. And then, at that time, they had a business agent by the name of Jaborotsky in 10. Great, big guy, boy, and he was rough. And he would come and he would go and threaten the proprietors and all of that type of a thing, get them out of here, and if I catch them in here, and he was liable to punch the musicians.
Oh, yeah, it was a -- well, people go into -- see, everything back in those days was muscle and force. Because
the joints were all owned by hoodlums and things like that. So it was a real rough deal for the musicians. But fortunately, as compared to today, --
